title: Fix catastrophic-backtracking regex in SourceCodeDisclosureWebInf and BigRedirectsScan
body:
## What
Replaces a redundant, backtracking-prone `regex` check with `contains_either` in two templates:

- `Security-Misconfiguration/SourceCodeDisclosureWebInf.yaml`: validate's `regex: ".*java.*"` → `contains_either: [java]`
- `Security-Misconfiguration/BigRedirectsScan.yml`: both `api_selection_filters` and `validate`'s `regex: ".*href.*href.*"` → `contains_either: [href]`

## Why
The engine evaluates `regex` via `Matcher.find()` (not `matches()`), so wrapping a pattern in leading/trailing `.*` never added any matching power — it only made the regex engine backtrack far more on large response bodies (each `.*` is a greedy quantifier that first consumes the whole input, then backtracks character by character).

Measured single-threaded, with no concurrency noise (via `RunSingleApi`, one call per template, full 888-template sweep), these two templates alone accounted for ~37% of the sweep's total time against a ~143KB payload (21.6s + 10.8s out of 87.2s), while contributing near-zero against a ~12KB payload. Excluding just these two templates, the other 886 templates showed essentially flat cost (~1.2x) between the two payload sizes — confirming this was a template-level regex bug, not a systemic payload-size cost.

## Behavior change
`BigRedirectsScan.yml`'s original regex required `href` to appear **twice** in the response body (an approximation for "looks like a list of multiple redirect links"). `contains_either` can only check presence, not count, so this relaxes the check to "href appears at least once." This relaxation was explicitly discussed and accepted as tolerable.

`SourceCodeDisclosureWebInf.yaml`'s change is behavior-preserving — a single-substring `.*java.*` check is exactly equivalent to `contains_either: [java]`.

title: [fix] #659 : Add Host Header Manipulation Test
body:
# Description

Closes [#659](https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/issues/659)

This pull request addresses Issue #659, which involves the addition of a new security test for Host Header Manipulation. The test checks whether an attacker can create or update an entity using this method, and it focuses on specific requirements:

🎯 Requirements:

- Filters: Applicable to APIs with GET query parameters or JSON body parameters.
- Execution: The test adds or replaces values in HTTP headers:

  -   Host: localhost if the Host header exists, or adds it as a new value.
  -   Host: 127.0.0.1 if the Host header exists, or adds it as a new value.
  -   X-Forwarded-For: evil-website.com
  -   X-Forwarded-Host: evil-website.com
  -   X-Client-IP: evil-website.com
  -   X-Remote-IP: evil-website.com
  -   X-Remote-Addr: evil-website.com
  -   X-Host: evil-website.com

- Validation: If the application responds with an exception trace or error response strings, it is considered a vulnerability.

The new test is structured and designed to verify security against Host Header Manipulation in various scenarios. It aligns with the objectives of Issue #659.

Please review this PR and provide feedback or merge it as appropriate.
